newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canadian Airlines crisis sparks Canada debate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian Airlines crisis sparks Canada debate.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp.'s struggle to survive has soared to the top of Canada's national agenda as the carrier's unionized employees and Canadian politicians debate how to keep the airline aloft.

The cash crisis at Canada's second largest airline has sparked ideological clashes and raised questions about whether the deregulation of the nation's airline industry will spell the demise of one of its biggest players.
"(Politicians) are to some extent trapped by their own ideology," said David Taras, a Canadian studies professor at the University of Calgary.
Taras said that western opposition members of parliament are constrained by their anti-government intervention philosophy from fighting for their constituents' jobs at Calgary-based Canadian.

Canadian said last week it faced oblivion early next year unless it could enact a tough program of employee wage rollbacks, route restructurings and reduced fees to 33 percent-owner AMR Corp. of Fort Worth, Texas.

Financial crises are nothing new to Canadian, which has not posted an annual profit since 1988 despite government-backed loans, layoffs, a C$700 million ($525 million) debt restructuring and a C$246 million ($185 million) cash infusion from AMR in the past five years.

Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson said much of the cash drain resulted from higher than expected jet fuel prices and overcapacity in Canadian domestic services. The plan aims to address the weaknesses without reliance on revenue growth.
Canadian is a major employer, especially in Western Canada, where disgruntlement over the eastern political and economic power base has long simmered.
The airline employs more than 8,100 workers in western provinces, not including staff at its Canadian Regional unit. The company has a total of 16,400 employees.

Western members of parliament in the ruling Liberal Party said Canadian was important to their local economies and must not be allowed to collapse. Such an event could cost the government western votes in an election expected next year.
But the federal goverment's focus -- which has won praise from Canadians and international bond-rating agencies -- is cutting the country's budget deficit.
Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said on Thursday he would not consider financial aid, at least until the company showed progress in its life-support plan.

"Without the success of a restructuring plan, there would be no point in offering a loan or guarantee or anything else," Anderson said. He also suggested that employees accept the plan's 10 percent pay cut, despite strong opposition from their big unions.

The unions, including the International Association of Machinists, which represents 5,300 workers, and the Canadian Auto Workers, which represents 3,700, have called on the federal government to bail out the company.
The IAM said the government should give C$70 million ($53 million) to Canadian, noting that Quebec-based Bombardier Inc. received an C$87 million ($65 million) interest-free federal loan in October.
The government should also reregulate the industry's pricing, routes and entrance of new carriers, the unions said. Anderson rejected the idea.
He said, however, that the government would entertain proposals from AMR to raise its stake in Canadian, which would require an exemption under transportation regulations.

Canadian said it would not ask for government money, and would instead hold fast to its own survival strategy, which carries a deadline for agreement from all participants before the end of this month.
